articles.title: Sign in to your mail
articles.summary: Sign in with your address and password; choose whether this is your own device or a shared computer.
steps: Open your organisation's mail address in a browser. The page says "Sign in to your mail" with your organisation's name.
Type your address (or just the part before @, on your organisation's own page) and your password, then press Sign in.
Under "This computer is", choose My own device (stay signed in) or Shared computer (signs out after 15 minutes idle).
If you set up two-step sign-in, type the code from your authenticator app, use your passkey, or use a backup code.
articles.tip: On a shared computer, always choose Shared computer: nothing is kept on it, and you are signed out when you leave it.
articles.keywords: login log in password signin

articles.title: Choose your language
articles.summary: Anjal speaks the languages your organisation has switched on.
steps: On the sign-in page, open the language menu at the top right and pick your language.
Once signed in, open Settings, then Language and time.
Choose your language, your time zone and how dates look, then save.

show.line: Your language, time zone and dates are here.

articles.keywords: tamil hindi malayalam marathi gujarati language time zone date format

articles.title: Find your way around
articles.summary: The rail on the left holds Today, your folders, Contacts, the dashboard and Settings.
steps: Today, at the top of the rail, shows your unread mail and what needs you first.
Below it are Inbox, Drafts, Sent, Scheduled, Archive, Junk, Trash and your own folders.
At the bottom: Dashboard, Organisation (for administrators), Settings and your initials, which open your account menu.
Press ? anywhere to see every keyboard shortcut, or Settings, Help, Take the tour again.

show.line: Everything starts from the rail.

articles.keywords: rail menu navigation tour

articles.title: Sign out, here or everywhere
articles.summary: Sign out from the account menu; sign out of every other device from Security.
steps: Click your initials at the bottom of the rail.
Choose Sign out.
To sign out on every other device, open Settings, Security, and press Sign out everywhere else.

show.line: Your account menu, with Sign out.

articles.keywords: logout log out signout shared computer

articles.title: Change the colours and density
articles.summary: Pick light or dark, a colour, how much fits on the screen, and how big everything is.
steps: Open Settings, then Appearance.
Under Light or dark choose Light, Dark or Follow the device.
Pick a colour, then choose Comfortable or Compact density and your layout (three panes, Focus or List only).
Under Size on screen choose Normal, 90% or 80% to make everything smaller. If Windows shows everything at 125%, 80% shows Anjal at its usual size.
Changes apply at once. Only you see them.

show.line: Theme, density and layout.

articles.keywords: dark mode light mode colour color theme density compact layout size zoom smaller bigger font text too big

articles.title: Use the keyboard
articles.summary: Press ? anywhere for every shortcut. The most used: j and k to move, e to archive, # to delete, r to reply.
steps: Press ? to open the shortcuts panel.
In a list: j and k move down and up, Enter opens, x ticks.
On a message: r replies, a replies to all, f forwards, e archives, # deletes, s flags.
Tips on the buttons name their shortcut, for example "Archive · e".
articles.keywords: keyboard shortcut keys hotkeys

articles.title: Start your day on Today
articles.summary: Today shows only your unread mail: what needs you first, everything else, then lists and notifications.
steps: After you sign in, Anjal opens on Today.
Needs you holds answers to your own mail, mail with you in To, and people you write to often. Each row says why.
Everything else follows; lists and notifications are folded into one line you can open or mark read.
The side shows what needs attention and your morning: what arrived since yesterday evening and what went to Junk.

show.line: Today: your unread mail, grouped by why it needs you.

articles.keywords: today home landing unread needs you

articles.title: Read and reply without leaving Today
articles.summary: Click a row: the letter opens beside the list, with a quick reply at its end.
steps: On Today, click a message. The letter and its envelope open beside the list.
Type in the box at the end of the letter and press Send, or Ctrl + Enter.
The next unread message opens by itself. Messages you dealt with stay in the list, faded, until you leave Today.
Press Full reply to write with formatting, attachments or more people.

show.line: Click a row below to read it here.

articles.keywords: quick reply ctrl enter next unread

articles.title: Open Anjal on the Inbox instead
articles.summary: If you prefer, Anjal can open on your Inbox rather than Today.
steps: Open Settings, then Mail.
Under Open Anjal on, choose Inbox.
Shared mailboxes always open on their Inbox.

show.line: Open Anjal on: Today or Inbox.

articles.keywords: start page landing inbox first

articles.title: Read your dashboard
articles.summary: Six pages of figures about your own mail: Overview, Mail flow, People, Replies, Safety and Storage.
steps: Open Dashboard from the rail.
Choose a page from the tabs, and a period at the top: Today, 7 days, 30 days, 90 days, 12 months or Custom.
Every card has a Chart and a Table switch; the table can be sorted and taken as CSV.
Every number opens the messages it counts.

show.line: Six pages, each with its own figures.

articles.keywords: dashboard figures charts statistics reply time storage

articles.title: Read a message and its envelope
articles.summary: The letter shows the subject and the text; the envelope beside it shows who sent it, to whom, the files and the stamps.
steps: Open a message. The letter is on the left, the envelope on the right.
The envelope's address block shows From, To and Cc; people outside your organisation are marked "· outside".
Enclosed lists the files, each with its type (PDF, JPG, DICOM...).
The stamps show what Anjal proved: a verified sender, mail that arrived encrypted, an original kept unchanged.
articles.keywords: envelope stamps from to cc attachments enclosed

articles.title: What the stamps mean
articles.summary: Green stamps are what Anjal could prove about a message.
steps: Verified sender: the sending domain's records (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) agree that this sender is who they say.
Arrived encrypted: the message came over an encrypted connection.
Original kept: Anjal keeps the exact message as it arrived, with its fingerprint, as proof.
No stamp means it could not be proved; be careful with links and attachments.
articles.keywords: verified encrypted original proof seal

articles.title: Reply, reply all or forward
articles.summary: Use the buttons at the end of the letter, or r, a and f.
steps: Open the message.
Press Reply (r), Reply all (a) or Forward (f).
When many people, or anyone outside your organisation, would get a reply all, Anjal asks first.
articles.keywords: reply all forward respond

articles.title: Flag a message to come back to
articles.summary: The flag marks a message; flagged mail is easy to find again.
steps: Open the message and press Flag in the envelope, or press s.
In a list, click the flag on the row.
Press it again to take the flag off.
articles.keywords: flag star mark important

articles.title: Archive or delete
articles.summary: Archive keeps mail you are done with, out of the Inbox; Delete moves it to Trash.
steps: Open the message, or tick it in a list.
Press Archive (e) to keep it out of the way, or Delete (#) to move it to Trash.
The bar at the bottom of the screen offers Undo for a few seconds.
Trash empties itself after its time (Settings, Mail, Empty Trash after).
articles.keywords: archive delete trash remove bin

articles.title: Undo what you just did
articles.summary: Archive, Delete, Move and Send can be undone from the bar at the bottom of the screen.
steps: After an action, the bar at the bottom says what happened.
Press Undo while it is shown.
For Send, the wait is set in Settings, Mail, Undo Send.
articles.keywords: undo mistake take back unsend

articles.title: Print a message, a conversation, or see the original
articles.summary: Print gives a clean page of one mail or of the whole conversation, with who printed it and when; Show original gives the message exactly as it arrived.
steps: Open the message and press Print in the envelope.
Choose This mail, or The whole conversation to print every mail of it in order.
Each page ends with "Printed by" your name and the time, the Message-ID, and your organisation's note if it set one.
Under More, choose Show original to see the raw message and download it.
articles.keywords: print printout paper conversation thread original raw source eml footer printed by

articles.title: Write a new message
articles.summary: Compose is two sheets: the letter for the subject and text, the envelope for who gets it and the files.
steps: Press Compose at the top of the rail, or c.
In the envelope, type the people in To and Cc; press + Bcc for blind copies. People outside your organisation are marked.
Write the subject and the text in the letter. The formatting bar is above the text.
Press Send (Ctrl + Enter). The bar at the bottom offers Undo for a few seconds.

show.line: Send, Send later and More are here.

articles.keywords: compose new message write email

articles.title: Add files
articles.summary: Drop files on the envelope or press Attach. Each file shows its type.
steps: In Compose, drag files onto the dashed area in the envelope, or click it to choose files.
Each file shows its type and size under Enclosed.
Your organisation may limit the total size of a message.
articles.keywords: attach attachment file upload pdf

articles.title: Send later
articles.summary: Choose when a message goes; it waits in Scheduled until then.
steps: In Compose, press the clock beside Send.
Pick a time, or type a date and time.
The message waits in Scheduled; you can change or cancel it until it goes.

show.line: The clock beside Send.

articles.keywords: schedule send later timer delay

articles.title: Expect a reply
articles.summary: Mark a message you need an answer to; Anjal shows it in Waiting for a reply.
steps: In Compose, switch on Expect a reply at the bottom of the letter.
After you send it, it appears in the dashboard's Replies page under Waiting for a reply until someone answers.
articles.keywords: follow up waiting reply reminder

articles.title: Use a template
articles.summary: Start a message from a template your organisation or you saved.
steps: In Compose, press More, then Templates, and pick one.
To make your own, write the message and choose More, Save as template.
Administrators can save a template for everyone.
articles.keywords: template canned reply standard letter

articles.title: Send one each
articles.summary: Send the same message to many people, each getting their own copy with their name.
steps: In Compose, put a group or many people in To.
Press More, then Send one each.
Each person gets their own copy; the copies go out over a few minutes.
articles.keywords: mail merge bulk personal copies

articles.title: Make a folder
articles.summary: Your own folders sit under the standard ones in the rail.
steps: Open Settings, then Folders and rules.
Type a name under Your folders and press Create.
A folder can be removed once it is empty.

show.line: Your folders and your rules.

articles.keywords: folder create new label organise

articles.title: File mail automatically with a rule
articles.summary: A rule moves, files or marks mail as it arrives.
steps: Open Settings, then Folders and rules.
Press Add rule, say which mail (from, subject, words) and what to do with it.
Rules run top first; the first that matches acts. They apply to mail arriving from now on.

show.line: Add rule is here.

articles.keywords: rule filter automatic move sort

articles.title: Use categories
articles.summary: A category is a coloured label; your organisation shares some, and you can add your own.
steps: Open a message and choose a category in the envelope.
To make your own, open Settings, Categories, and press New category.
A sender can be filed in a category automatically.
articles.keywords: category label colour tag

articles.title: Keep junk out, or let a sender in
articles.summary: Mark a message as junk, or tell Anjal a sender is always welcome.
steps: On a message in Junk, press Not junk to move it back and trust the sender.
On unwanted mail, press Mark as junk.
Open Settings, Junk and senders to see who is always or never sent to Junk.
Junk empties itself after its time.

show.line: Always or never to Junk.

articles.keywords: spam junk block allow sender whitelist

articles.title: Search your mail
articles.summary: Type words, or use filters: from:meera has:attachment last week.
steps: Type in the search box at the top of the list, or press /.
Add filters by typing them: from:name, has:attachment, after:2026-10-01, before:..., in:all, or words like "last week".
Each filter shows as a chip under the box; press its × to take it off.
Search looks in the folder you are in; in:all, or All folders, looks everywhere.
articles.keywords: search find filter from has attachment date

articles.title: Save a contact
articles.summary: Contacts give names to addresses and come first in suggestions.
steps: Open Contacts from the rail.
Press + to add a person, or save a sender from any message's envelope.
Contacts outside your organisation are marked "· outside".
Import and export with vCard or CSV.

show.line: People, Groups and Organisation.

articles.keywords: contact address book people save

articles.title: Make a group
articles.summary: A group is many people as one recipient.
steps: Open Contacts, then Groups.
Press +, name the group and list the addresses, one a line.
Write to the group from its page, or type its name in To.
articles.keywords: group distribution list team

articles.title: Find a colleague
articles.summary: The Organisation tab lists everyone in your organisation.
steps: Open Contacts, then Organisation.
Type a name in the search box.
Click a person to write to them.
articles.keywords: colleague directory staff organisation

articles.title: Change your password
articles.summary: A long password is the best one: 15 characters alone, or 12 with two-step.
steps: Open Settings, then Security.
Type your current password and the new one twice, then press Change password.
Anjal refuses passwords known from leaks; a sentence of a few words works well.

show.line: Password, two-step and devices.

articles.keywords: password change reset forgot

articles.title: Turn on two-step sign-in
articles.summary: After your password, Anjal asks for a code from your phone or your passkey.
steps: Open Settings, Security, and press Set up two-step sign-in.
Scan the picture with your authenticator app, or type the key into it.
Type the code it shows to finish, then save your backup codes somewhere safe.

show.line: Set up two-step sign-in is here.

articles.keywords: 2fa two factor authenticator otp code
articles.org: Your organisation may require two-step for administrators or everyone.

articles.title: Add a passkey
articles.summary: A passkey on your phone or computer can be your second step.
steps: Open Settings, Security.
Press Add a passkey and follow your device.
Next time, choose Use a passkey at the second step.
articles.keywords: passkey fingerprint face webauthn

articles.title: Keep backup codes
articles.summary: Backup codes let you in when your phone is not with you.
steps: Open Settings, Security, Backup codes.
Press Make new backup codes, then Download or print them.
Each code works once. Keep them away from your computer.
articles.keywords: backup codes recovery lost phone

articles.title: Set a recovery address
articles.summary: A forgotten password is reset with a code sent to your personal address.
steps: Open Settings, Security, Recovery address.
Type a personal address (not this one) and save.
If you forget your password, press Forgot password on the sign-in page; the code goes there.
In an organisation, a password set this way signs you in but leaves your mail locked until an administrator restores it; you get a mail when it is done.
articles.keywords: forgot password reset code personal email

articles.title: Your mail is encrypted
articles.summary: In an organisation, your mail is encrypted so that only you, and your administrators through the organisation's recovery key, can read it - not Anjal.
steps: Your password opens your mail. If you sign in with a passkey, Anjal asks for your password once on that device.

If your password is set without the old one (forgotten, or reset by your administrator), your mail stays locked until an administrator of your organisation restores it; you get a mail when it is done.
Who mailed whom stays visible, so that mail can be delivered; subjects, the mail itself, files and your contacts do not.
articles.keywords: encrypted encryption locked unlock open my mail restore passkey privacy
articles.org: Administrators: Organisation, Encryption holds the recovery sheet, the people waiting for a restore, and the switch for Anjal's break-glass key.

articles.title: See where you are signed in
articles.summary: Signed-in devices lists each browser; sign one out, or all others.
steps: Open Settings, Security, Signed-in devices.
Each device shows where and when it was last used.
Press Sign out beside one, or Sign out everywhere else.
articles.keywords: devices sessions signed in sign out lost

articles.title: Mail to people outside the organisation
articles.summary: Compose warns when someone is outside your organisation, and says so again when there is an attachment.
steps: In Compose, a warning under the addresses names anyone outside your organisation.
When there is an attachment as well, the warning says so. Check the addresses before you send patient information.
In a message you received, the envelope marks outside people "· outside".
Your organisation decides who may write outside.
articles.keywords: outside external patient privacy confidential
articles.org: Your organisation may limit who can write outside.

articles.title: Originals kept as proof
articles.summary: Anjal keeps every message exactly as it was sent or received, with its fingerprint.
steps: Every message you send or receive is kept as it was, with a SHA-256 fingerprint.
The Original kept stamp on the envelope says so.
Your organisation's retention rules decide how long; a legal hold keeps everything.
articles.keywords: evidence proof original legal hold audit

articles.title: Use Anjal on your phone
articles.summary: The same address works on a phone: Today, Inbox, Compose, Search and More at the bottom.
steps: Open your organisation's mail address in the phone's browser and sign in.
The bar at the bottom has Today, Inbox, Compose, Search and More.
On a message, the envelope strip under the back bar opens the full envelope.
articles.keywords: mobile phone android iphone

articles.title: Read your list offline
articles.summary: On your own device, Anjal can keep your list, locked with an offline code.
steps: Open Settings, Security, Offline mail.
Set the offline code (at least 6 characters).
When there is no connection, open Anjal and type the code to see your list.
Mail is never kept on a shared computer.
articles.keywords: offline no internet connection

articles.title: Invite people
articles.summary: Invite each person; they choose their own password from the link.
steps: Open Organisation, then People.
Press Invite people, type the name and address (and a personal address for the link).
Give them the link, or let Anjal send it; it works once, for 7 days.
To invite many at once, import a CSV with a Name and an Address column.

show.line: Invite people is here.

articles.keywords: invite add user person staff account

articles.title: Set up your organisation
articles.summary: The Set up page lists six steps; each shows when it was done.
steps: Open Organisation; until everything is done it opens on Set up.
Do the steps in order: Name and logo, Add your domain, Prove the domain, Invite your first people, Shared mailboxes, Applications that send mail.
The step to do now has its button; finished steps show their date.

show.line: Six steps to set up.

articles.keywords: setup onboarding checklist start organisation

articles.title: Add and prove a domain
articles.summary: Your domain's DNS records tell the world your mail is real.
steps: Open Organisation, Domains, and add your domain.
Publish the records Anjal shows (MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC) at your DNS provider.
Press Check the records; each turns green when it is right. Anjal checks them every day.

show.line: Your domains and their records.

articles.keywords: domain dns mx spf dkim dmarc records

articles.title: Make a shared mailbox
articles.summary: A shared mailbox (reception@, opd@) is read and answered by several people.
steps: Open Organisation, Shared mailboxes.
Add one, then give people read only, read and send, or manage.
People open it from the rail; it always opens on its Inbox.
articles.keywords: shared mailbox reception team inbox delegate

articles.title: Set sign-in rules
articles.summary: Decide two-step, idle times and password length for your organisation.
steps: Open Organisation, Sign-in and sessions.
Choose who must use two-step, how long idle sessions last, and a longer password if you wish.
Rules apply at each person's next sign-in.
articles.keywords: policy two-step required idle session timeout

articles.title: Retention and legal hold
articles.summary: How long mail is kept, and holding a mailbox when a case needs it.
steps: Open Organisation, Retention.
Set how long Junk and Trash keep mail, and copies passed to applications.
Place a legal hold on a mailbox: nothing is deleted from it until the hold is lifted.
articles.keywords: retention legal hold keep delete compliance

articles.title: Read the activity log
articles.summary: Every sign-in and administrator action, with a chain that shows nothing was changed.
steps: Open Organisation, Activity log.
Filter by person or action, and export as CSV.
Press Check the chain to prove no entry was changed or removed.
articles.keywords: audit log activity history who did

articles.title: Add an application
articles.summary: Each system that sends mail gets its own address and send-only keys.
steps: Open Organisation, Sending systems, and press Add an application.
Give it a name, what it does, and the one address it sends as.
Make a key. It is shown once: copy it into the application.
Rotate a key by making a new one, switching the application over, then ending the old one.

show.line: Sending systems, with Add an application.

articles.keywords: application key api smtp integration his

articles.title: Send from an application
articles.summary: Applications sign in on port 587 with their key and send as their own address.
steps: Open Organisation, Sending systems, Applications, for the sample.
Point the application at your mail host on port 587, with STARTTLS.
Sign in with the key's user name and the key; send as the application's address.
Press Send a test to check delivery end to end.
articles.keywords: smtp 587 port curl integration send

articles.title: Find out what happened to a message
articles.summary: Messages shows every message an application sent, with every attempt and the receiving server's own reply.
steps: Open Organisation, Sending systems, Messages.
Search by address, subject or message id; filter by status and application.
Click a message: the timeline shows each try, the server, the TLS used and its exact reply.
While it is still being tried you can press Try now or Stop trying; .eml downloads the original.

show.line: Every message, with its tries.

articles.keywords: delivery delayed bounced failed status tries log

articles.title: The do-not-send list
articles.summary: Addresses that bounced hard or were given up on three times are not sent to again.
steps: Open Organisation, Sending systems, Do not send.
Anjal adds an address after a hard bounce (the mailbox or domain does not exist), or when it gives up three times.
The API answers suppressed for such an address; mail sent by SMTP is marked Suppressed.
Add an address yourself, or remove one that works again. People's own mail is never held.
articles.keywords: suppression bounce do not send blocklist

articles.title: Webhooks and Replay
articles.summary: Mail to an application's +tag addresses is posted to its webhook; failed deliveries can be replayed.
steps: Open Organisation, Sending systems, Webhooks.
Each delivery shows the time, the webhook's answer and the tries.
When a delivery failed, press Replay once the webhook is working again.
articles.keywords: webhook inbound replay callback

articles.title: Check your sending domain
articles.summary: SPF, DKIM, DMARC and MTA-STS decide whether receiving servers trust your applications' mail.
steps: Open Organisation, Sending systems, Domains and DNS.
Each record shows Correct, Missing or Differs.
Fix a record at your DNS provider, then check again from Domains.
articles.keywords: spf dkim dmarc mta-sts dns deliverability

articles.title: How an account is made
articles.summary: Four paths lead to a mailbox: an individual invited by User management, an individual filled in by User management, an organisation person invited by their administrator, and an organisation person filled in by the administrator. In every path the mailbox exists only after Submit, the Terms are emailed, the first mail is the Welcome mail, and nobody under 18 is accepted.
steps: Invited: the invitation email has one link that works once, for 7 days. The registration page asks for what is still missing and checks the username live.
Filled in by an administrator: they type everything, including the password, and give it by hand. At first sign-in nothing opens until the Terms are accepted, and a new password is asked for.
Submit creates the mailbox. The Terms go to the personal email address, and the Welcome mail is the first mail in the new Inbox.
Individuals choose their own username; an organisation's administrator chooses it, and it cannot be changed later.
articles.tip: Your date of birth is asked once, to be sure you are 18 or over. It is kept with your account and never shown on your mail.
articles.keywords: register registration invite invitation join username under 18 date of birth terms welcome

figure.caption: How an account is made: four paths, and what changes later.

articles.title: Accept the Terms of Use
articles.summary: Every account accepts Anjal's Terms of Use and Disclaimer once: on the registration page, or at first sign-in when an administrator filled in the account.
steps: Read the Terms and the Disclaimer; both are linked at the foot of every sign-in page, and always at /terms and /disclaimer.
Tick both boxes and press Continue. Until then nothing in the mailbox opens.
A copy of the Terms is emailed to your personal address the moment your account is made, so you have them in writing.
articles.keywords: terms of use disclaimer legal accept agreement

articles.title: Sign in to more than one account
articles.summary: Up to five accounts can be signed in together in one browser, and the account menu switches between them without typing a password again.
steps: Open the account menu (your initials at the foot of the rail) and choose Add another account.
Sign in to the other account as usual. Both now appear in the menu; the one with the tick is open.
Choose a name in the menu to switch. Sign out of this account leaves the others signed in; Sign out of all signs out every one.
articles.tip: On a shared computer, use Sign out of all.

show.line: Your account menu: switch, add another, sign out.

articles.keywords: switch account several accounts multiple add another sign out of all

articles.title: Change the name on your mails
articles.summary: The name beside your address on every mail you send. In an organisation it is your first and last name; an administrator may allow nicknames.
steps: Open Settings, Profile.
Type the name under Name on mails and press Save.
If your organisation has not allowed nicknames, the box is fixed to your first and last name.

show.line: Name on mails is here.

articles.keywords: display name nickname from name sender name profile phone
articles.org: Your organisation decides whether nicknames are allowed.

articles.title: Forward mail to another address
articles.summary: A rule can send a copy of matching mail to any address; the original always stays in your mailbox. A rule can also be run over mail you already have.
steps: Open Settings, Rules, and press Add rule.
Say what the rule matches, then fill in Forward a copy to.
Press Save. Tick Apply to older mail to forward what already matches, up to 200 messages.
articles.tip: Forwarded mail carries Resent headers and the Anjal forwarding mark, and is never forwarded on more than three times.

show.line: Forward a copy to is in every rule.

articles.keywords: forwarding forward copy redirect auto-forward
articles.org: An organisation's administrator decides whether mail may be forwarded outside the organisation.

articles.title: Set an out-of-office reply
articles.summary: While you are away, everyone who writes to you gets one reply, once, with your subject and text. Automatic mail and mailing lists are never answered.
steps: Open Settings, Away, and tick Send an away reply.
Choose from when and until when, who gets it (everyone, your organisation, or your contacts), and write the subject and the text.
Press Save. A bar above the Inbox shows the reply is on, with Turn off beside it.
articles.tip: The reply stops on its own on the Until day.

show.line: Away reply is here.

articles.keywords: out of office vacation holiday auto reply autoreply away message leave
articles.org: Your organisation may limit away replies to people inside it.

articles.title: Snooze a message
articles.summary: Snooze puts a message out of sight until a time you choose, then brings it back to the top of the Inbox, marked Back.
steps: Open the message, or tick it in the list, and press Snooze.
Choose Later today, Tomorrow, This weekend, Next week, or pick a date and time.
Snoozed mail waits in the Snoozed folder, shown in the rail while it has anything in it. Unsnooze brings a message back at once.
articles.keywords: snooze remind later postpone hide until tomorrow

articles.title: Block a sender
articles.summary: Blocked senders' mail is dropped on arrival, silently: nothing reaches any folder, and the sender is not told.
steps: Open a message from the sender and press Block sender.
Settings, Senders, Blocked lists everyone you have blocked, with how many messages were dropped, and Unblock.
To keep a sender's mail but out of the way, use Always to Junk instead.

show.line: Blocked senders are listed here.

articles.keywords: block blocked sender discard silent drop spam unwanted

articles.title: Unsubscribe from a mailing list
articles.summary: When a message comes from a list that says how to leave it, an Unsubscribe button appears on the message. Anjal sends the request for you.
steps: Open the message and press Unsubscribe.
Anjal sends the list's unsubscribe mail, or presses its one-click link, and marks the message Unsubscribed.
Mail that still arrives after a week can be blocked instead.
articles.keywords: unsubscribe mailing list newsletter leave list-unsubscribe

articles.title: Download or delete your data
articles.summary: Everything in your account can be downloaded as one file, and you can ask for the account to be deleted (the DPDP Act gives you both rights).
steps: Open Settings, Your data, and press Prepare a download. The file is ready within a few minutes and can be downloaded for 7 days.
The file holds every message as .eml, your contacts, rules, profile and activity, with a README that explains the layout.
To delete the account, press Ask to delete and type your address. Your administrator confirms it; the address is never reissued, and evidence is kept for its legal period, then erased.

articles.title: The application API for developers
articles.summary: Applications send mail, read what happened to it, and receive mail over HTTPS at https://<your mail host>/api/v1/. JSON in, JSON out; the full description is at /api/v1/openapi.json.
steps: Send: POST /api/v1/messages/email with X-Api-Key and a body of from, to, subject, text and/or html (or a template). The answer is 202 with the send's id. Set Idempotency-Key: a retry with the same key and body gets the first answer, never a second mail.
Status and events: GET /api/v1/messages/{id}, GET /api/v1/events?since=<last seq>, or webhooks. A 429 says which window is full and when to try again (Retry-After).

Signing: the string is the method, the path and query, the Unix time and the hex SHA-256 of the body, joined by new lines. Sign it with your ECDSA P-256 key (SHA-256) and send Anjal-Key-Id, Anjal-Timestamp and Anjal-Signature (base64url). The inbox always needs it.
Decrypting inbox mail in Python (cryptography): key = priv.decrypt(b64(wrappedKey), OAEP(MGF1(SHA256()), SHA256(), None)); mail = AESGCM(key).decrypt(b64(iv), b64(ciphertext) + b64(tag), None).

In Node: key = crypto.privateDecrypt({key: priv, oaepHash: 'sha256'}, wrappedKey); d = crypto.createDecipheriv('aes-256-gcm', key, iv); d.setAuthTag(tag); mail = Buffer.concat([d.update(ciphertext), d.final()]).
For .NET, the Anjal.Client package does all of this: AnjalClient, InboxMessage.Decrypt and WebhookVerifier.
articles.tip: Never put patient details in tags or metadata: they are kept readable so that you can search them.
